headline: Oregon's last no-limits governor race: $40 million and a familiar winner
dek: Christine Drazan and Gov. Tina Kotek raised more than $40 million before Oregon's new contribution limits take effect. Late national money and union checks paid for a TV fight over Trump, abortion and taxes. Kotek won by 9.6 points.
summary: Kotek beat Drazan by 9.6 points in a $40 million rematch; Merkley outraised his opponent 28-to-1 and won easily.

paras.text: This year's race for Oregon governor was the last of its kind. The 2026 midterms will mark the last election in Oregon in which political donors can cut major checks without limits thanks to a 2024 state law. Donors took advantage. Gov. Tina Kotek, a Democrat, and state Sen. Christine Drazan, the Canby Republican she beat in 2022, raised a combined $40,490,871.20, according to their 2026 ORESTAR account summaries available on October 31. ORESTAR is the secretary of state's campaign-finance database.

Kotek won the rematch, 1,000,012 votes to 819,566, a 9.6-point margin in the Associated Press count published by The New York Times. Drazan sent FOX 12 a concession statement saying "I reached out to Governor Kotek to wish her well."

The totals vary by source and date. The Oct. 31 ORESTAR summaries showed Drazan at $21,536,886.94 and Kotek at $18,953,984.26. By another count, as of Nov. 2, Drazan had received $21.5 million in campaign contributions and spent about $22.2 million. Kotek had received about $19 million and spent $20.2 million. The Oregon Journalism Project put Kotek's total higher, at the $22 million her campaign raised. The Watch could not reconcile the figures.

Drazan's largest backer came in late. On Oct. 8, OPB reported that she reported $1 million from the Republican Governors Association, then her largest single donation to date. In the end, according to Central Oregon Daily, the association gave her $5.75 million in the last month before the election. The Daily Tidings put the October figure at $5.25 million. Either way, it was lower than the more than $7 million the national group gave her 2022 campaign. Her other top donors included Don H. Jones Jr., president of an Ashland-based auto dealership company, the Eugene-based wood manufacturer Murphy Plywood, the Salem-based construction contracting company K & E Excavating and the Republican-aligned Bring Balance to Salem PAC. The Associated General Contractors' $700,000 check in late August is the single largest donation they have made to a political candidate since their first political donations were recorded in 2006. Phil Knight, the Nike co-founder who backed Drazan in 2022, was missing from her list this time. Instead he gave $1 million to her opponent in the Republican primary, the former Portland Blazer Chris Dudley.

Kotek drew on unions and her national party. Her supporters included public employee unions, a $5 million boost from the Democratic Governors Association, and a political action committee representing Oregon's nurses. The political committee of the Service Employees International Union Local 503 provided about $1.5 million to her campaign. The largest single check of the cycle went to a union PAC. On September 16, 2026 the North Coast States Regional Council of Carpenters gave $10 million to Building a Stronger Oregon. That committee has given Kotek $755,000, according to Portland Civic Lab's review of the filings. A union official told OPB the money "is to support multiple candidates and multiple measures from today moving forward."

Kotek's campaign kept most of its paid messaging on Washington. Its first general-election spot, "Looks Like," highlights Governor Kotek's record of standing up to Donald Trump and opened the campaign's statewide multi-million dollar paid media program. In "Suffer," a TV ad, a doctor says Drazan backs Trump's Medicaid cuts. In "Abortion – Always," a digital ad, a narrator says she "sponsored bills to take away abortion rights, even jail abortion providers." Filings reviewed by Portland Civic Lab show Kotek's committee spending $2.32 million for broadcast, though those records stop on Oct. 12.

Drazan's ads were about Oregon's economy. In September she ran a TV spot about Tina Kotek's yearslong history of giving special tax breaks to data centers while repeatedly raising taxes. In another ad she said "The politicians sat by and watched while the mills closed and jobs disappeared". Near the end she addressed the Democratic message directly. She looked directly into the camera and promised she wouldn't ban abortions, she wouldn't cut healthcare and she wouldn't let Washington, D.C., control Oregon.

Outside groups did not play much of a role. The newly formed ACLU of Oregon Democracy PAC spent $574,000 to produce two mailers that contrast the positions of Kotek and Drazan on voting rights, immigration and abortion. A spokeswoman called the mailers voter education, not an endorsement. Stand for Children Oregon PAC reported a $75,000 independent digital ad buy in support of Tina Kotek.

Going by spending, the side that spent more lost. Drazan spent about $2 million more than Kotek and finished 9.6 points behind. The campaign had been expected to be close. A DHM Research poll for OPB found Drazan was leading Kotek among likely voters by 47% to Kotek's 46%. Kotek still ran 4.8 points behind Oregon's 2024 presidential margin. OPB's post-election analysis gave much of the credit to the national mood. It said the national Republican backlash voters delivered Tuesday helped buoy Kotek to another four-year term despite deep dissatisfaction with the direction the state is heading. Readers can decide how much the ads tying Drazan to Trump added to that.

The U.S. Senate race was never close in money or votes. FEC data has not yet been read for The Watch's data block. In filings compiled by Legis1, through Oct. 14, Merkley reported $8,729,810 in cumulative receipts and $6,621,250 in cash on hand, while Smith reported $311,174 in receipts and $44,198 in cash on hand. VoteLog's tally found $0 of independent expenditures disseminated after the May 19, 2026 primaries. Sen. Jeff Merkley beat state Sen. David Brock Smith 1,081,831 to 719,976, a 19.4-point margin and 5 points better than the 2024 presidential result.
